name: Crossing the Chasm
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Gap Where Promising Technologies Go to Die
lesson.summary: Geoffrey Moore's chasm describes the specific, dangerous gap between early adopters and the early majority, a gap that many well funded technologies never cross, and one that quantum computing has not yet reached, let alone cleared.
lesson.body:
Geoffrey Moore's 1991 book Crossing the Chasm refined the adoption curve by identifying a danger zone between early adopters and the early majority. Moore argued the two groups want fundamentally different things, not just different risk tolerance. Early adopters are visionaries chasing a strategic breakthrough and will tolerate an incomplete product if the underlying capability is genuinely novel. The early majority are pragmatists who want a complete, safe solution, proven by reference customers like themselves, integrated with existing tools, and backed by a mature vendor ecosystem. A product built to excite visionaries often fails to satisfy pragmatists, and crossing requires deliberate repositioning, not just more time.

This chasm is why many well funded technologies with a devoted early adopter following never reach durable mainstream success. They sell to the adventurous first slice of the market, generating real revenue, testimonials, and investor enthusiasm reflected in valuations, then plateau once that segment is exhausted, because the early majority does not yet trust the product enough to switch its daily operations onto it. From outside, a company stuck in the chasm can look, for a while, indistinguishable from one still ramping up, which is exactly what makes it dangerous to investors extrapolating from recent growth.

Quantum computing's position relative to the chasm follows directly from QC Stuck at TRL 2-3. A technology generally needs to be well past the middle of the TRL scale before it can even build an early adopter base, let alone attempt the harder move to the early majority. Current revenue, examined under D-Wave Revenue Reality, looks much more like pre-chasm activity: research collaborations, pilot programs, and government contracts with organizations willing to experiment with unproven technology, rather than repeat purchases from a widening base of ordinary commercial customers.

This has a quantifiable implication for reading a growth number. Suppose a company's revenue grows from 8 million to 16 million dollars in a year, a headline 100 percent growth rate, since 16 is double 8. Before treating that as mainstream adoption, ask whether the growth came from selling deeper into the existing pool of early adopter labs and pilots, a finite pool, or from genuinely new early majority customers making repeat, reference driven decisions. The first kind of growth can look identical to the second for years, right up until the early adopter pool saturates and growth abruptly stalls, the classic signature of hitting the chasm rather than crossing it.

Together, this batch builds a coherent picture: real but small, services heavy revenue, stretched valuations compared within an equally stretched peer group, exit paths narrowed toward acqui-hires, a venture model that can rationally tolerate most individual losses, hardware still largely at early laboratory maturity, and even in an optimistic future, a difficult, unproven move still ahead from early adopters to a mainstream market. None of that proves quantum computing will fail. It means today's valuations require several separate, uncertain things to go right in sequence, not just one.
